passage: At the Sunrise children's home, each small bed had a chart taped beside it. Sumit's had three pictures: a toothbrush, a glass of milk, a pair of shoes. Every morning he went down them in order. Brush, brush, spit. Milk, all of it, even the skin on top. Then shoes, side by side in the wooden rack by the door. Each time, Sister Mercy pressed a star into one of his boxes. Ten stars meant a trip to the big park. Sahil, in the next bed, counted with him. "Eight." Sumit's eyes went wide. "Two more!" He lined his shoes up extra straight.

qa.q: What three pictures were on Sumit's chart?
qa.a: A toothbrush, a glass of milk and a pair of shoes.

qa.q: What does Sumit lining up his shoes extra straight suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He felt excited and eager, because only two more stars stood between him and the big park 😊

qa.q: What could help Sumit if he forgets a step one morning?
qa.a: He could look at the pictures again or ask Sister Mercy; the chart works because the same three steps come in the same order every day.

qa.q: How might the chart look to Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil counts the stars with Sumit, so Sahil seems to share the excitement and may be keen on the park too.

grounding: Shows a child working down a picture chart of morning tasks, a star for each, toward ten stars and a park trip.

passage: This summer I'm staying with Francis's family, so I see the sticker chart on the fridge every morning. First Francis brushes and comes out with foam still on the chin. Sachin, the big brother, hands over a sticker. Then the milk: Francis pinches the nose and gulps it down to the last drop. Another sticker. Then the school shoes go into the rack by the door, toes pointing in. Sticker three. Last night Francis counted the row out loud: seven. After this morning there are ten, and ten means the park. I can't tell what Francis thinks of the milk, but nobody skips a step.

qa.q: Who hands Francis the stickers?
qa.a: Sachin, the big brother, hands over the stickers.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis wants the park trip?
qa.a: Francis gulps the milk to the last drop while pinching the nose and counts the stickers out loud, which suggests Francis is eager and excited to reach ten.

qa.q: What would help if one step, like the milk, gets too hard?
qa.a: The family could talk it over with Francis while keeping the same order; the chart works because each small step earns something visible.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the chart?
qa.a: Sachin hands out each sticker, so he is part of the routine and probably enjoys seeing the row grow toward the park.

grounding: Shows a child following a chart of morning tasks, a sticker for each, until ten stickers earn a park trip.

passage:
"Beans again?" Varun poked the plate.
"Beans and carrots," said Amma. "Eat up."
Varun looked at the green pile, then at Deepika, who was reading a comic.
"Amma. If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?"
Amma raised her eyebrows. "All of them? The carrots too?"
"All. Carrots too."
"Two stories, then. Deepika reads one, I read one."
"Hey!" said Deepika. Then she shrugged. "Fine. But I pick mine."
Varun ate the beans in big fast bites, making faces, and held up his clean plate. "Two stories!"

qa.q: Which vegetables were on Varun's plate?
qa.a: Beans and carrots.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he ate in big, fast bites?
qa.a: His faces show he didn't enjoy the beans, but he felt determined and excited about getting two stories.

qa.q: What might make Varun's deal fairer for everyone?
qa.a: He could ask Deepika too, since she is one of the readers; naming the price and the prize worked because everyone knew the terms.

qa.q: How does Deepika see the deal?
qa.a: Deepika is surprised to be pulled into it, but agrees as long as she gets to pick her own story.

grounding: Shows a child making an explicit deal, eating all the vegetables in exchange for two bedtime stories.

passage: Note for Gopika's parents, Wednesday evening. Dinner went well today, which surprised me. Gopika saw the palak and started to push the bowl away, then stopped and asked, "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" I said yes, if the bowl was empty. It took a while, with a few sighs, but it was empty. Madhav wanted the same deal for his peas, so I agreed for him too. We read two stories each on the big bed. Both were asleep by nine. You may want to keep using this; both of them seemed proud of their clean bowls.

qa.q: What vegetable did Gopika start to push away?
qa.a: Gopika started to push away the palak.

qa.q: What do Gopika's sighs over the bowl suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Gopika found the palak hard going and felt reluctant, but stayed determined because two stories were promised.

qa.q: Which other approach could the note-writer try on nights when Gopika doesn't bargain?
qa.a: State a simple rule up front, like 'vegetables first, then stories', so the deal is clear without Gopika having to ask.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see the deal?
qa.a: The note-writer was surprised it worked so well and suggests the parents keep using it, since both children seemed proud.

grounding: Illustrates a child naming a clear price and prize, all the vegetables for two stories, which makes the deal explicit.

passage:
Monday. Playtime ended and Tanuja's blocks stayed all over the floor. At bedtime her sticker box was empty. "Why no sticker?" Papa just pointed at the blocks.
Wednesday. When Papa called, "Playtime's over," Tanuja stopped mid-tower. "If I put my toys away, I get a sticker," she whispered, and dropped every block into the tub. Sticker.
Saturday. Her little brother Vaibhav kept driving his car under the sofa. Tanuja tugged his sleeve. "Toys away first, then sticker. See?" She pointed at her chart, which now had four shiny stars.

qa.q: How many stars were on Tanuja's chart by Saturday?
qa.a: Her chart had four shiny stars.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when her sticker box was empty on Monday?
qa.a: She seemed puzzled and disappointed, asking 'Why no sticker?' until Papa pointed at the blocks.

qa.q: What else could help Vaibhav learn the same link?
qa.a: He could have a small chart of his own, or Tanuja could tidy with him; she learned the rule by seeing the link between tidying and the sticker.

qa.q: How might Papa see the change from Monday to Saturday?
qa.a: Papa only had to point once; by Saturday Tanuja was tidying by herself and teaching Vaibhav, which probably makes evenings easier.

grounding: Shows a child holding the rule that tidying toys earns a sticker and acting on it the moment playtime ends.

passage: Playtime ended in a rush: Nana's car honked at the gate, and there were only a few minutes before they left for the fair. The floor was covered with Nikita's toy animals and her cousin Chinmay's train tracks. Chinmay ran for his sandals. Nikita stood still, thinking out loud. "If I put my toys away, I get a sticker. If I just go, no sticker." She scooped the lion, the elephants and the giraffe into the basket, fast. Mumma stuck a star on the chart by the door as Nikita ran out. Chinmay's tracks were still on the floor.

qa.q: Why did playtime end in a rush?
qa.a: Nana's car honked at the gate, and there were only a few minutes before they left for the fair.

qa.q: Why did Nikita stop and think out loud before running out?
qa.a: She wanted the sticker and felt torn between rushing out and tidying, so she said the rule aloud and chose to tidy first.

qa.q: What might help Chinmay remember to tidy next time?
qa.a: A small chart with the same rule, or a warning a few minutes before the car comes; Nikita tidied because she clearly understood what the sticker was for.

qa.q: How might Mumma see Nikita's choice?
qa.a: Mumma sees Nikita tidy even in a rush and sticks the star on at once, so she seems pleased the rule is understood.

grounding: Illustrates a child saying the if-then rule for a sticker aloud and tidying her toys as soon as playtime ends, even in a hurry.

passage:
Tuesday evening. Kavitha skipped putting her shoes in the rack and ran up to the roof instead. She found the first star and squeezed her eyes shut. "Star, please put five stickers on my chart." She was sure it would work.
Wednesday morning. She raced to the fridge. The same three stickers as before. "The star forgot!" she wailed. Her brother Sachin shrugged. "Stars don't have stickers."
Saturday. Sachin's chart was full, so Appa took him to the park. Kavitha, who had kept wishing instead of doing her jobs, had four stickers. She watched from the gate and kicked at the dust.

qa.q: What did Kavitha ask the star for?
qa.a: She asked the star to put five stickers on her chart.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling on Wednesday morning?
qa.a: She felt shocked and upset to find the same three stickers, and wailed that the star forgot.

qa.q: What would you change first for Kavitha?
qa.a: Help her link jobs to stickers, like putting her shoes in the rack every evening; wishing felt easier but never added a sticker.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the star wish?
qa.a: Sachin thinks stars don't have stickers, so to him the wish seems silly, and he is the one who gets the park trip.

grounding: Shows a child trusting a wish on the first star to add stickers instead of doing the routine, and missing the reward.

passage: It had rained all day in Kochi, and the clouds would not move. After dinner Aadhya pressed her face to the window, waiting for the first star. "When it comes, I'll wish for six stickers," she told Kishore, her older brother. "You still have to brush your teeth for a sticker," Kishore said. Aadhya didn't move. At last a star peeped through, and she whispered her wish. She fell asleep on the window seat without brushing. In the morning she ran to the chart. No new stickers at all, not even the brushing one. She stared at the empty boxes, lip trembling.

qa.q: What did Aadhya plan to wish for?
qa.a: She planned to wish for six stickers.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she stared at the empty boxes?
qa.a: Her trembling lip shows she felt disappointed and let down, because she had trusted the wish to fill her chart.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya have done while waiting for the star?
qa.a: She could have brushed her teeth first and then wished, so the routine still earned a sticker even if the wish did nothing.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel seeing Aadhya in the morning?
qa.a: Kishore had warned her about brushing, so he might feel sorry for her and hope she remembers the routine next time.

grounding: Illustrates a child trusting a star wish over the routine, waiting instead of brushing, and finding no stickers in the morning.

passage: Leela had been sticking stars on her chart for days, and still no zoo trip. Her classmate Kavitha had already been and brought back a photo with a camel. "It's never going to happen," Leela grumbled, flopping onto the floor of their Mumbai flat. Then she sat up and dragged the chart to Aai at the stove. "How many more stickers?" Aai wiped her hands. "Let's count the empty boxes." Their fingers moved together: one, two, three. "Three," said Leela. She held up three fingers, then marched off to put her shoes in the rack. "That's one," she called.

qa.q: How many empty boxes were left on Leela's chart?
qa.a: Three empty boxes were left.

qa.q: Why did Leela flop onto the floor and grumble?
qa.a: She felt impatient and discouraged because the zoo trip seemed never to come, especially after Kavitha had already been.

qa.q: What else could help Leela keep the goal in view?
qa.a: She could count the empty boxes with Aai each evening or cross them off as she goes; asking turned a vague wait into three clear steps.

qa.q: How might Aai see Leela's question?
qa.a: Aai stopped cooking to count with her, so Aai seems to see it as a good moment to show Leela how close she is.

grounding: Shows a child, unsure how far off the reward is, asking her mother how many stickers remain and counting three together.

passage:
"Mama, is it cake day yet?"
"Not yet, Uma."
"But I did SO many stickers."
Uma kicked the chair leg. Siddharth, on the floor with his blocks, copied her kick.
"Hmm," Uma said. She pulled the chart off the fridge. "Mama. How many more stickers?"
"Come, let's count together." Mama put her finger on the first empty square. "One..."
"Two," said Uma. "Three!"
"Three more, and we bake the chocolate cake."
"Three is small!"
"Three is small," Siddharth agreed from under the table.
Uma put the chart back and went straight to tidy her crayons.

qa.q: What will Uma and Mama bake when the chart is full?
qa.a: They will bake the chocolate cake.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she kicked the chair leg?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and impatient, because she had done so many stickers and still didn't know when cake day would come.

qa.q: What could Mama do so Uma doesn't have to wait to ask next time?
qa.a: Mama could draw a little cake in the last box, so Uma can count the gap by herself whenever she wonders.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth, watching Uma?
qa.a: Siddharth copies her kick and her words, so he seems to pick up her mood and share her cheer at the end.

grounding: Illustrates a child asking her mother how many more stickers are needed and counting three together, which makes the goal concrete.

subtype: Approach: giving up after a miss [Pitfall]
passage:
"Sabina, sticker time! Did you drink your milk?"
"No."
"Brush your teeth?"
"No. The chart's finished."
Mehak looked up from her homework. "Finished? It's only half full."
"I missed Monday and Tuesday. It's broken now." Sabina pushed the chart under the sofa with her foot.
"So no park?" Mehak asked.
"No park. Ever."
Abbu came over and pulled the chart out, dusting it off. "Two empty days don't break it. Look, we start counting again from today. Milk?"
Sabina looked at the chart, then at Abbu. "...One sticker?"
"One sticker."

qa.q: Which days did Sabina miss?
qa.a: She missed Monday and Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Sabina push the chart under the sofa?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and ashamed after missing two days, as if the whole chart was broken and there was no point trying.

qa.q: What else could help Sabina after a missed day?
qa.a: Starting the count again from today, as Abbu does, or simply carrying on past the gap; one miss doesn't have to cancel the goal.

qa.q: How does Mehak see Sabina's decision?
qa.a: Mehak is surprised, since the chart is only half full, and her questions show she thinks giving up is too quick.

grounding: Shows a child declaring the chart finished after two missed days until a parent restarts the count.

subtype: Approach: giving up after a miss [Pitfall]
passage: Class note, Friday. Bidisha was away on Wednesday and Thursday, so her helper chart has two empty boxes. This morning she looked at it, said, "My chart's finished," and would not water the plants or stack the mats. Sabina offered her the watering can twice; Bidisha shook her head and sat by the window. At pickup I showed her mother the chart. Her mother crouched down and said, "Let's count from today. Today is box one." Bidisha stacked the mats right there, with her mother, and got her sticker. The chart will keep counting from today.

qa.q: Which days was Bidisha away?
qa.a: She was away on Wednesday and Thursday.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling as she sat by the window?
qa.a: She seemed discouraged and hopeless about the chart, as though two empty boxes meant she had already failed.

qa.q: What else could the note-writer try if Bidisha gives up like this again?
qa.a: Show her straight away that the count can restart today, rather than waiting until pickup; her mother's 'box one' is what got her moving.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Bidisha refusing the watering can?
qa.a: Sabina offered twice and was turned down, so Sabina may have felt puzzled or a little shut out.

grounding: Illustrates a child treating two missed days as total failure until a parent restarts the count from box one.

passage: It was almost time for the temple fair, and Trisha had only one sandal. "Go back through the day," Ajji always said. So she did. First the bedroom: under the cot, only a lizard. Then the verandah, where she had shelled peas with Keerthana that morning: a pea pod, no sandal. Then the gate, where they had played hopscotch in the dust. There, half buried beside the gatepost, was the pink strap. Trisha pulled it out, banged the dust off, and ran to catch up with Keerthana on the road.

qa.q: Where did Trisha find the sandal?
qa.a: Half buried beside the gatepost.

qa.q: What does Trisha's run down the road suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed relieved and happy, eager to reach Keerthana and the fair with both sandals on.

qa.q: What else could Trisha do so she doesn't lose a sandal before an outing?
qa.a: She could keep both sandals together by the door; going back through the day in order worked because it narrowed the search to three places.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the search?
qa.a: Keerthana had been part of Trisha's day, so Keerthana may have waited on the road, glad the fair wasn't missed.

grounding: Shows a child finding a lost sandal by going back through her day in order: bedroom, verandah, then the gate where she played.

passage: Ulla had one red rain boot on and one sock foot, and the kindergarten bus came at eight. Papa Liam checked the clock. "Think back," he said. Ulla closed her eyes. "Bedroom. Then the porch. Then the gate, where I jumped in the puddle." She padded to the bedroom first. Nothing under the bed. Then the porch, where the rain jackets hung. Only a wet umbrella. Then the garden gate, and there it was, lying on its side in the big puddle, full of water. Ulla tipped it out, squelched her foot in, and made the bus just in time.

qa.q: Where did Ulla find the boot?
qa.a: By the garden gate, lying on its side in the big puddle, full of water.

qa.q: What might Ulla have felt as she squelched her foot into the wet boot?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved to have found it and to catch the bus, even if the wet boot was uncomfortable.

qa.q: What else could Ulla do so this doesn't happen before the bus?
qa.a: Put both boots by the door straight after playing outside; retracing worked, but it only just beat the bus.

qa.q: How might Papa Liam experience the morning?
qa.a: Watching the clock, Papa Liam was probably tense, and then relieved that thinking back found the boot so quickly.

grounding: Illustrates a child retracing her day in order, bedroom, porch, then the gate, to find a lost boot.

passage:
"Mummy, I can't find my shoe."
"Which one?"
"The left one. The sparkly one."
Mummy kept plaiting Yamini's hair. "Where did you last have it?"
Ritu thought. "At the door... no. I took them off to jump on the bed."
"Then?"
"Then I went to see Yamini's fish."
"Check both places, one at a time."
Ritu ran to the bed. Nothing. Then to the fish tank in Yamini's room.
"Found it! It was under the tank table!"
Yamini laughed. "My fish was guarding it."

qa.q: Which shoe had Ritu lost?
qa.a: The left one, the sparkly one.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she shouted 'Found it'?
qa.a: She felt relieved and happy that Mummy's question led her straight to the shoe 😊

qa.q: What could Ritu try on her own next time before calling Mummy?
qa.a: She could ask herself Mummy's question, 'Where did I last have it?', and then check each place one at a time.

qa.q: How does Yamini seem to see the search?
qa.a: Yamini finds it funny and jokes that the fish was guarding the shoe.

grounding: Shows a child telling her mother she can't find her shoe, and the mother's question about where she last had it giving the search a structure.

passage: Dear Elizabeth Miss, sorry Mehak was late today. At 8:10 she came to me with one shoe on and said, "Mummy, I can't find my shoe." I was packing lunch, so I only asked, "Where did you last have it?" She stood still, then said, "I took them off to feed the cat on the balcony." She went to the balcony, looked behind the plant pots, and came back with it. It took four minutes, but she did the searching herself. I have told her that from now on shoes come off at the door. Mehak's mother

qa.q: Why had Mehak taken off her shoes?
qa.a: She took them off to feed the cat on the balcony.

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt when she came back with the shoe?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and relieved, having done the searching herself after just one question.

qa.q: What else could help Mehak avoid losing shoes before school?
qa.a: Taking shoes off only at the door, as her mother has now told her, so there is one place to look.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth Miss see the late arrival after reading the note?
qa.a: Elizabeth Miss would understand the four-minute delay and might see it as a small lesson in searching rather than carelessness.

grounding: Illustrates a child telling her mother she can't find her shoe, and the mother's question giving the search a structure.

passage: After nap time at the daycare, Deepak had only one shoe. Devika, the helper didi, was busy with the babies. Deepak lay on his mat and stuck one foot in the air. "I'm the shoe," he told himself. "Deepak kicks me off. Whoosh! Where would I go?" He rolled across the floor, the way a kicked shoe might, and stopped by the reading corner. "Under the sofa! Shoes like dark places." He peeked under the little sofa. There it was, beside a lost crayon. He waved it at Devika, grinning.

qa.q: What was lying beside the shoe under the sofa?
qa.a: A lost crayon.

qa.q: What does Deepak's grin suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased that his game of being the shoe had found it all by himself.

qa.q: Which other approach could Deepak try if pretending doesn't help?
qa.a: He could ask Devika where shoes usually end up after nap time, or check each corner in turn; pretending worked because it made him picture where a kicked shoe rolls.

qa.q: How might Devika see Deepak waving the shoe?
qa.a: Busy with the babies, Devika would likely be relieved and amused that he found it himself.

grounding: Shows a child pretending to be the missing shoe and imagining its path, which leads him to look under the sofa.

passage: I was reading on the divan when Rekha and Preeti came looking for Rekha's school shoe. They had already checked the rack twice. Then Rekha did something funny. She put her hands together like a shoe and said, 'I'm the shoe. Where would I go?' She walked her hand-shoe across the carpet, along the side of the sofa, and let it slide down. 'I'd hide in the dark!' The two of them flopped on the floor and looked under the sofa. Preeti shrieked and pulled out the shoe, covered in dust. I don't know how Rekha thought of it, but it worked faster than their shouting.

qa.q: How many times had they checked the rack?
qa.a: They had checked the rack twice.

qa.q: Why might Rekha have pretended to be the shoe?
qa.a: After the rack came up empty twice she seemed frustrated and wanted a fresh way to think; the game made her curious instead of stuck.

qa.q: What else could Rekha try if her pretend journey doesn't find the shoe?
qa.a: She could think back to when she last wore it, or ask an adult; imagining the shoe's path worked here because it led to the dark space under the sofa.

qa.q: What was the search like for Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti joined in, flopped down and shrieked on finding it, so for Preeti it turned into an exciting game instead of a chore.

grounding: Illustrates a child pretending to be the missing shoe and asking where it would go, which leads to looking under the sofa.

passage: From my window across the courtyard I could see Jasleen sitting on her front step in one shoe. Her mother, Zainab, called from inside, 'Did you look under your bed?' Jasleen shook her head. 'It ran away. It'll come back if I wait here.' She sat with her chin on her knees, watching the gate. Zainab came out twice, holding a bag and checking her watch. Then the wedding car honked. In the end Zainab carried Jasleen out in one shoe and one sock. I can't say whether Jasleen truly believed it, but she kept looking back at the step.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen sit to wait?
qa.a: On her front step, in one shoe.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling as she kept looking back at the step?
qa.a: She may have felt worried and sad, still hoping the shoe would come home now that she had left.

qa.q: What could help Jasleen next time a shoe goes missing?
qa.a: Searching the places she had been, starting under the bed, instead of waiting; waiting at the door left her going out in a sock.

qa.q: How does Zainab seem to experience the wait?
qa.a: Zainab keeps checking her watch and finally carries Jasleen out, so she seems hurried and stressed by the lost time.

grounding: Shows a child insisting a lost shoe ran away and waiting at the door for it instead of searching.

passage:
Friday. Jaya's new sandal was gone. "It ran away," she told Santosh, her big brother. "It'll come home if I wait." She sat by the door with her doll till dinner.
Saturday. Still one sandal. Jaya waited again, even when Santosh called her to fly kites. Her bare feet rested on the hot step.
Monday. Santosh moved the washing basket and out fell the sandal. Jaya grabbed it. "See? It came home." Santosh opened his mouth, then closed it. Jaya had missed the kites, and now it was time for school.

qa.q: Where did the sandal turn up on Monday?
qa.a: It fell out when Santosh moved the washing basket.

qa.q: Why did Jaya keep waiting by the door even when called to fly kites?
qa.a: She trusted that the sandal would come home and felt hopeful, perhaps worried that leaving would spoil it.

qa.q: What would you change first for Jaya?
qa.a: Help her look in a few places in order, like under the washing basket, instead of waiting; the waiting cost her the kite flying.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Jaya's 'It came home'?
qa.a: Santosh knows he found it under the basket, but he stays quiet, perhaps not wanting to argue with his little sister.

grounding: Illustrates a child believing a lost sandal ran away and will return if she waits, so waiting replaces searching for days.
